sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** and **Does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** (one problem): The sidebar highlights "Billing" (64–264, 185–227) as the current page. The heading at (304,112) says "Account settings", and the main area shows a summary of four areas, with Billing only third (305–1215, 443–569). The user can't tell which page they're on. If they clicked "Billing" they land on a general overview and have to hunt for billing in the third card. If they're on an overview, the nav is pointing to the wrong place. The labels also don't match. The sidebar lists "Security", but the card covering signed-in devices is called "Sessions". "Members" and "Integrations" have no card at all. So the sidebar and the cards look like two different site maps. This goes against Nielsen 4, consistency and standards (one term means one thing on the screen), and Nielsen 1 (the page heading should name the current page, matching the nav). The fix: make the nav state, the heading and the content agree. Either mark no nav item as current and keep "Account settings" as a true overview, or open on Billing with "Billing" as the heading and the billing content. Use the same name for the same area in both places ("Security" or "Sessions", not both). Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?**: The left sidebar (78–264, 112–345) and the card stack both work as an index of settings areas, and three of the labels are the same: Profile, Notifications, Billing. The page offers two ways to reach the same places, side by side, and the user has to work out whether "Profile" in the sidebar and "Edit" on the Profile card go to the same place. That's screen space and attention spent on a second menu (Nielsen 8, aesthetic and minimalist design; "Redundancy and duplicate controls"). The fix: give each its own job. The sidebar handles navigation and the main area holds the selected section's actual settings. Or drop the sidebar and let the cards be the index, with all six areas listed. Convention. Weight: major. It shares a root with finding 1, and fixing one will likely fix the other.

**What's working.**
- Every card's copy says plainly what the area does for the user, often with a concrete fact: "Your plan renews on 1 March", "You are signed in on three now". So each card already tells the user whether they need to act, without opening anything.
- Everything shares one restrained mood: neutral greys, one blue accent, the same radius and outline-button style throughout. It reads as a single, calm admin tool with no collage feel.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether clicking "Billing" in the sidebar really leads to this overview, or this is a stale or wrong nav state in the capture. Check this in the live app, because finding 1's severity depends on it.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 5 yes, 3 no (every element does a job; each kind of element looks the same everywhere; each heading names its section)

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on "Account settings" (top left of the content, about 304–537 × 98–128), the largest and boldest text on the screen. It then drops down the four bold card headings (Profile, Notifications, Billing, Sessions) and over to the four outlined buttons on the right, which all carry the same weight. The highlighted "Billing" item in the sidebar is a weaker second stop. This reads as a SaaS account settings overview for a workspace member. Assumed job: let the user find a setting group and open it quickly.

What matters first:
- One element stands clearly above the rest: **yes**. The page title is about 28 px bold against roughly 17 px card headings, and nothing else competes. The four identical cards repeat on purpose, which suits an index of settings, so it is not monotony.
- Each level of text can be told apart at a glance: **yes**. There are about four levels: the title, then card headings and the brand (both about 17–18 px bold), then sidebar items (about 15 px), then grey body and meta text (about 14 px). The brand and the card headings share a size, but they are one level in two separate regions, not two levels that collide. The sidebar and body differ in colour and role.
- Headings also differ in weight, form, or colour: **yes**. The card headings are semibold and near-black, and the descriptions are regular weight in mid-grey.

No line is no or unsure, so I opened no entries.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One clear place to start.** "Account settings" is the only large type on the screen, about 1.6× the card headings, so the eye knows where to begin. Everything else sits a clear step below it. Keep that gap when revising, and don't push the card headings up toward it.
- **Card headings stand out by weight and colour, not only size.** Bold near-black headings sit over regular grey descriptions, so each card's heading is readable at a glance even though the size step is small (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger). This is why the four cards scan as a clean list.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Every line of this section passes. Two lines were close calls:
- **Space between groups:** each card has about 45 px of space above its title, but the cards are only about 16 px apart. The card borders still separate the groups clearly, and each title sits tight to its description (about 28 px).
- **Empty space:** each card has a wide empty gap between its description and its button. That is the usual layout for a settings row. The page also has two large, deliberate open areas: the sidebar column and the band below the last card.

If the director wants a taste note: the cards could lose about 10–15 px of top and bottom padding each. That would tighten the list and bring the fourth card's button higher without crowding anything. This is minor taste, not a defect.

**What's working.**
- **One strict grid.** The logo and the selected Billing highlight share x=64. The page title and the cards share x=304. The workspace label in the header and the card right edges share x=1216. All four buttons line up on one right edge at x=1190. Each column and edge appears only once, so the page reads as ordered at a glance. Keep these edges when you add rows or buttons of other widths.
- **The page title lines up with the first sidebar item.** "Profile" in the sidebar and "Account settings" sit on the same line (around y=112), so the sidebar and the main column start together and the eye moves straight from one to the other.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Bash isn't available in this session, so I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so the crop script would have printed `no crops` anyway. I worked from the whole image.

**Walk (Text)**
- Body text large enough: yes. The card descriptions look about 14 px, against nav items of about 15 px and button labels of about 14 px bold. They are secondary lines in a settings list, and the gap is within a pixel.
- Captions and labels: yes ("Workspace: Harbour Studio" looks about 14 px).
- Plain reading face: yes.
- One typeface plan: yes. One sans family, Inter-like.
- Weight at small sizes: yes.
- Contrast: yes. The grey descriptions (about #4b5563 on white) and grey nav items (on #f3f4f6) look well above 4.5:1.
- Text over image: yes (there is none).
- Line length: yes. Every line is one short line of 60 to 70 characters.
- Leading: yes. Single lines; the heading-to-description gap is tight and grouped.
- Multi-line heading: yes (there is none).
- Flush left: yes.
- Justified text: yes (there is none).
- Rag: yes (no paragraphs wrap).
- Widows and runts: yes.
- Heading breaks: yes.
- Paragraph marks: yes.
- Left edges: yes. Card titles and descriptions share a crisp edge at x≈329.
- Long text chunked: yes.
- Mixed case: yes.
- Emphasis: yes.
- Large heading spacing: yes. "Account settings" at about 28 px bold looks evenly set and not loose.
- Kerning: yes.
- Tracking: yes.
- Capitals letterspaced: yes (no strings of capitals).
- Ligatures: yes ("fi" in "Notifications" and "file" is at small size).
- Real cuts: yes.
- Quotes and dashes: yes (none used).
- Tabular figures: yes (no numeric columns).
- Real type: yes.
- Nothing clipped: yes.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there was nothing to open in step 5.

---

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One copy note that the checklist has no line for, for the director to weigh. **Taste/defect, minor:** the Billing description at about (329, 521) reads "Your plan renews on 1 March. The invoice goes to the address on file." This is a date and billing commitment the viewer will act on, and "the address on file" can be read two ways: a billing email address or a postal address. The date also has no year and the line gives no amount. That matters less on a settings page, but a viewer checking when they'll be charged, and where the invoice goes, has to click through to find out. Fix: name the destination and the amount, e.g. "Your plan renews on 1 March 2027 for £X. We'll email the invoice to billing@…".

**What's working.**
- The type system is restrained. There are about four sizes: a 28 px page title, a 17 px bold card title, a 15 px nav and 14 px descriptions and buttons. Fine steps are made with weight and grey rather than extra sizes (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger), so each card reads as a title and a quiet explanation at a glance.
- Every description is one short, plain sentence in the viewer's terms ("Your name and photo appear on comments and in the member list"). This tells the viewer what each setting does to them, not just its category.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (working notes). First read: the eye lands on "Account settings" and then moves down the four white cards. This is a SaaS settings screen with cool, quiet neutrals, and the only colour is the blue on the buttons and on the selected nav item. I assume it is an account settings overview for workspace users.

Color:
- Small palette: yes (one cool gray range plus one blue)
- Strong colour kept to a small area: yes (blue only on button text and borders and the Billing nav pill)
- Clear value range: yes (near-black headings, mid-gray body text, white cards on a light gray page with borders)
- Warm forward, cool back: yes (all cool, nothing needs to come forward through warmth)
- Matching colours look the same: yes (the button blues match each other and the nav blue)
- No vibrating edges: yes
- Status colours keep their usual meaning: yes (blue means interactive or selected)
- Colour never carries meaning alone: yes (the selected nav item also has a pill shape and bold weight)
- Dark theme gray: yes (not a dark theme)

No line is no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Colour is kept for things you can act on.** The one blue appears only on the four outlined buttons (Edit, Manage, View invoices, Review) and on the selected "Billing" item in the side nav. Everything else is gray, so anything blue reads at once as something you can click or something that is selected. Keep that rule if more colour is added. Don't put blue on headings or decoration.
- **The light-to-dark range holds the structure.** Headings are near-black, descriptions mid-gray, the cards white, and the page behind them light gray. The layout still reads in grayscale, and the colour doesn't have to do the structural work.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. There's a sidebar menu and four action buttons.

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening, such as the current page or step, progress, or loading?** No. The sidebar marks "Billing" as the current item (pale blue fill and bold blue text, about x 64–264, y 185–228). But the page is titled "Account settings" (x 304, y 112) and is an overview of four cards starting with Profile. The two location cues disagree, so the viewer can't tell which page they're on. They may think they clicked Billing and landed somewhere else, or that the Billing card is the only part that matters. Why it matters: a visible current-state cue only helps when it's accurate (Nielsen, heuristic 1; Laubheimer, NN/g "Menu-Design Checklist", guideline 5). Fix: make the menu and the page heading name the same place. Either add an "Overview" or "Account" item to the sidebar and mark that one on this page, or make this page the Billing page. If this is a capture glitch (state left over from another page), it's fine once the menu marks the right item. **Defect. Major**: the menu's one job here is to tell people where they are, and it tells them wrong.

2. **Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?** No. The sidebar lists six sections: Profile, Notifications, Billing, Members, Integrations, Security. The overview has four cards: Profile, Notifications, Billing, Sessions.
   - "Sessions" (card at y 587–713) has no sidebar item. The viewer has to guess whether it lives under Security.
   - Members, Integrations and Security have no card, so the overview looks complete but isn't.
   - The header says "Workspace: Harbour Studio" (top right) while the title says "Account settings". Billing and Members usually belong to the workspace and Profile to the person, so the viewer can't tell whether a change here affects only them or the whole team. Billing is the case that matters most.
   
   The viewer can't build a reliable map of the settings: which items are the same thing, what's missing, and how far a change reaches (Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, ch. 2, conceptual model). Fix: give every section one name, used the same way in the menu and on the cards ("Security" containing "Sessions", or rename one to match). Show every section in the overview or none. Split or label account settings versus workspace settings. **Defect. Major**: this page is a hub, and its job is to show how the settings are organised.

3. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?** No. The card descriptions explain what a setting is for instead of showing its current value:
   - Profile (y 232) describes where your name and photo appear but shows neither.
   - Billing (y 520) says "the address on file" without showing the address, and gives no plan or price. Its only action, "View invoices", doesn't let you change that address.
   - Notifications doesn't say what is set now.
   
   To check one value, the viewer has to click into a section. Sessions gets this right with "You are signed in on three now". Fix: show the current value on each card (avatar and name, plan and price, billing address, notification mode), and give Billing a button for what its text raises ("Change billing address"). This is **taste and common sense**: the Tognazzini source is not on the approved list. **Minor.**

**What's working.**
- The four actions are all outline buttons of equal weight, each on the right edge of its own card. This is an index of equal destinations, so no single filled primary button is the right choice. Each button also sits right beside the setting it opens.
- The button labels name what will happen ("View invoices", "Review" next to the line about signing out of devices), so they make sense in context. The outlines are dark blue on white, which looks like it clears 3:1.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the menu items and buttons show a visible keyboard focus indicator (at least 2 px, 3:1). People use settings pages from the keyboard, so check this in a browser.
- Whether the header sticks on scroll and covers focused controls.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 3 no (shows where the user is; puts what is needed next in front of them; grouping and names show how parts relate), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)
